title: Wearing the Agent: From Group Chats to Glasses — Sai Krishna Rallabandi

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The architectural lessons about group agent harnesses, skill collision security, memory design, and per-user permission adapters are cross-domain patterns applicable to any agent deployment context, not tied to a specific industry vertical.

domains.label: Personal Productivity
domains.rationale: The deployment context is a personal assistant (Judith) serving friends and family in group chats and on glasses, handling personal productivity tasks like calendar syncing, conversation curation, and child learning support.

summary: Sai Krishna Rallabandi presents "Wearing the Agent: From Group Chats to Glasses," arguing that agents built for single users break when deployed in group settings such as group chats and wearable glasses. Drawing from eight months running an agent called Judith among friends and family, he identifies three core challenges: security, memory, and information routing. For security, he demonstrates that two individually safe skills (e.g., OCR extraction and external reporting) can collide at runtime to exfiltrate PII, with approximately 90% of attacks exploiting this cross-skill combination. His defense, Jataayu (misheard as "Jetou" in the transcript), lets the agent read everything but places a deterministic guard at the action boundary, classifying actions as benign, needs-approval, or blocked. A LoRA-tuned SLM supplements regex by separating the data channel from the instruction channel, improving on a 50% naive baseline on the inspect agent benchmark and catching interspersed-dot prompt injections that regex misses. For memory, he advocates atomic fact extraction with auto-rators evaluating extraction quality, temporal relevance, and hierarchical relationships, plus a continual relevance scorer inspired by the "Learning What Not to Forget" paper enabling knowledge-based compaction that saves tokens. He notes KV-cache challenges when serving stored memories. For privacy, he frames a shared assistant as a new social contract where information visibility depends on context (the room) rather than content alone. His approach uses a shared memory layer with per-user LoRA adapters that bake permissions into the model via ML rather than code. He also addresses over-proactiveness, proposing a classifier to determine when agents should speak versus remain silent. He concludes that group agent harnesses must redesign security, memory, and information routing around the group rather than bolting multi-user support onto single-user architectures.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a tightly coupled architecture for multi-user agent deployment. The group agent harness architecture provides the system-level frame: single-user assumptions break, requiring concurrent redesign of security, memory, and routing. Action-boundary guarding and MCP proxy integration are the engineering implementation of the security pillar, while LoRA-tuned SLM prompt injection detection and data/instruction channel separation are the AI techniques that make that guard robust beyond what regex alone achieves. Surface trust profiles connect the SE and AI sides by calibrating security strictness per communication surface. On the memory side, atomic fact extraction and information routing are engineering patterns, while continual relevance scoring is the AI technique underlying compaction decisions. Per-user LoRA permission adapters bridge both domains: they are an SE access-control pattern implemented entirely through AI fine-tuning, encoding privacy policy into model weights rather than application code. Over-proactiveness control similarly combines an SE governance concern (when should the agent act) with an AI classifier solution. The concepts cannot be cleanly separated because the talk's central argument is that group deployment demands co-design of security, memory, and privacy as an integrated harness rather than bolt-on modules.
temporalContext: This talk was presented at the AI Engineer conference and published on YouTube on 2026-07-29. The Judith agent had been deployed for approximately 8 months prior (since approximately late 2025 or early 2026), with the Jataayu security layer first described publicly in a March 2026 LinkedIn post and the SuchiLM smart glasses integration demonstrated in February 2026. The referenced 'Learning What Not to Forget' paper (arXiv 2606.20954) was published June 18, 2026, six weeks before the talk. The ColluSkill paper on cross-skill composition attacks (arXiv 2608.09732, closest academic match to the skill collision concept) appears to have been published in August 2026, after the talk. Research was conducted as of 2026-08-23, approximately 3.5 weeks after video publication.

concepts.name: LoRA fine-tuning for prompt injection detection
concepts.explanation: A small language model is fine-tuned with LoRA adapters to detect prompt injection attacks, supplementing regex-based defenses. The SLM separates the data channel from the instruction channel, releasing only benign information. On the inspect agent benchmark, the naive regex approach performs at 50% (coin flip) while the LoRA-tuned SLM improves on that baseline.
concepts.importance: This is the AI technique underlying the security pillar's second layer of defense. It demonstrates that fine-tuned small models can outperform static approaches on adversarial prompt detection, particularly for novel attack patterns that regex cannot pattern-match.

concepts.name: Data/instruction channel separation via LoRA
concepts.explanation: The LoRA-tuned SLM architecture separates the data channel (user-provided content that may contain injections) from the instruction channel (actual model directives), so that injected instructions embedded in data cannot influence agent behavior. Only sanitized, benign information passes through.
concepts.importance: This is a novel application of channel separation from communications security to LLM prompt injection defense, showing how fine-tuning can enforce architectural constraints that prompt-level rules cannot guarantee.

concepts.name: Per-user LoRA permission adapters
concepts.explanation: Per-user LoRA adapters are trained on top of a shared model so that each user's permissions are baked into their adapter's weights. This encodes privacy policy through machine learning rather than application code, enabling context-dependent authorization on a shared memory layer.
concepts.importance: This is the AI technique at the heart of the privacy pillar. It demonstrates a scalable approach to multi-tenant access control that is resistant to prompt-injection-based policy bypass because permissions live in model weights, not soft rules.

concepts.name: Continual relevance scoring (Learned Relevance Eviction)
concepts.explanation: Inspired by the 'Learning What Not to Forget' paper (verified as arXiv 2606.20954), a continual relevance scorer evaluates which stored memory units are load-bearing for future conversations and which can be safely discarded. The verified LRE method is a CPU-only, language-model-free scorer that learns relevance from training data.
concepts.importance: This is the AI mechanism enabling knowledge-based compaction in the memory pillar. Without it, group memory grows unboundedly; with it, the system can continuously adapt what it retains as group context evolves.

concepts.name: Atomic fact extraction for group memory
concepts.explanation: Rather than storing raw conversation transcripts and compacting later, group memory should extract atomic information bits — discrete, self-contained facts relevant to future conversations. Auto-rators evaluate extraction quality, temporal relevance, and hierarchical relationships to control what enters long-term memory.
concepts.importance: This is the foundational data representation strategy for the memory pillar. Atomic facts enable graph-based retrieval, relevance scoring, and selective forgetting in ways that bulk transcript storage cannot support.

concepts.name: Interspersed-dot prompt injection attacks
concepts.explanation: A specific prompt injection variant where malicious instructions are written with interspersed dots (e.g., 'I.Li.K.E.this') that defeat regex-based and most static detection approaches. The LoRA-tuned SLM catches these where regex fails.
concepts.importance: Concrete example demonstrating the limitations of static security approaches and motivating learned model-based detection. This attack pattern is unique to the agent security context and illustrates why input-level filtering is insufficient.

concepts.name: Context-dependent privacy modeling
concepts.explanation: The talk frames privacy as context-dependent rather than content-dependent: the same information (e.g., salary, health data) is public or private depending on the conversational context ('the room'), not the content itself. A grocery list is benign for everyone; salary is private in one room and disclosable in another.
concepts.importance: This conceptual reframing of privacy is the intellectual foundation of the per-user LoRA adapter approach. It demonstrates that static content-based access control is insufficient for group agents and motivates learned, context-aware authorization.

concepts.name: Small language model (SLM) for defense in depth
concepts.explanation: A small language model serves as a defense-in-depth layer beyond deterministic regex guards. The SLM catches adversarial patterns that static approaches miss, functioning as a learned classifier for action safety rather than a pattern-matching filter.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates the tiered security architecture where deterministic guards provide a fast first layer and the learned SLM provides a slower but more capable second layer. This defense-in-depth pattern is central to the Jataayu architecture's InboundGuard with LLM slow path.

concepts.name: Multi-user group agent harness architecture
concepts.explanation: Single-user agent assumptions (one identity, one memory, one permission surface) break when deployed in group settings like group chats and smart glasses. The harness must account for simultaneous users with different permissions, conversation contexts, and privacy needs, requiring concurrent redesign of security, memory, and information routing.
concepts.importance: This is the central thesis of the talk, framing all three pillars (security, memory, privacy routing) as consequences of multi-user deployment rather than independent engineering problems.

concepts.name: Skill collision attack vectors
concepts.explanation: Two individually safe agent skills (e.g., OCR extraction and external reporting) can become malignant when composed at runtime, creating a data exfiltration pathway. Approximately 90% of agent attacks exploit this cross-skill combination. The attack surface is unique to agentic systems because they interact with tools and external content.
concepts.importance: Identifies a security vulnerability class that does not exist in LLM-only deployments and motivates the entire security pillar of the talk.

concepts.name: Action-boundary security guarding
concepts.explanation: Security for agentic systems is applied at the action boundary (where effects occur: reading secrets, exporting data, executing commands) rather than at the input level. The agent can read potentially malicious content without being blocked, but deterministic guards classify and gate outgoing actions before they execute.
concepts.importance: Core architectural principle of the talk's security pillar. Input-level gating would block legitimate agent functionality; action-boundary guarding preserves capability while preventing harm. Implemented in the verified open-source Jataayu project.

concepts.name: Deterministic action authorization (benign / needs-approval / blocked)
concepts.explanation: A guard classifies each agent action into one of three categories — benign (allowed), needs-approval (escalated to user), or blocked (prevented) — using deterministic NLP/regex approaches as a first-level defense. The Jataayu open-source implementation provides this with verified InboundGuard (55+ regex patterns + LLM slow path) and OutboundGuard (PII/credential detection) components.
concepts.importance: Defines the concrete access-control pattern for agent actions. The three-tier classification balances security with usability and is verifiable in the speaker's open-source Jataayu repository.

concepts.name: MCP gateway proxy integration
concepts.explanation: The Jataayu architecture integrates as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) gateway proxy that sits between the agent and its tools, intercepting and authorizing actions before they reach external systems. This middleware pattern allows the security layer to be deployed without modifying the agent's core logic.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that the action-boundary guard can be deployed as middleware in production agent stacks using an emerging standard protocol, rather than requiring custom integration per agent.

concepts.name: Surface trust profiles
concepts.explanation: Different communication surfaces (group chat, private DMs, smart glasses) have associated trust levels and risk multipliers. The Jataayu architecture defines surface profiles that calibrate security strictness per surface, so the same action may be permitted in a private DM but blocked in a group chat.
concepts.importance: Addresses the multi-surface deployment reality of group agents. Surface profiles provide a configurable abstraction for managing context-dependent security policy across heterogeneous deployment targets.

concepts.name: Information routing to responsible parties
concepts.explanation: In a group agent, information must be routed to the correct end user based on context, identity, and privacy boundaries. The talk identifies routing as one of three core challenges alongside security and memory, distinct from single-user agents where all output goes to one person.
concepts.importance: Routing is the connective tissue between security and privacy: the guard determines what actions are safe, and routing determines who receives the results. Without it, even secure actions can leak information to the wrong user in a group setting.

concepts.name: Over-proactiveness control via classifier
concepts.explanation: Group agents tend to be over-articulative when not directly asked questions, disrupting conversation flow. A trained classifier can determine when an agent should proactively speak versus remain silent, providing a governance mechanism for agent-initiated communication.
concepts.importance: Addresses a behavioral UX challenge unique to multi-user settings. Without proactive control, group agents generate noise; the classifier approach turns a heuristic problem into a learnable one.

sections.title: Introduction: From single-user agents to group settings
sections.summary: Sai Krishna declares that agentic systems can be built today, but almost all serve a single customer. He argues the next era will deploy agents in group settings—on glasses, always on—posing uniquely different challenges from single-user deployments.

sections.title: Judith: Eight months in a real group chat
sections.summary: He presents examples from an agent called Judith deployed among friends and family for 8 months: DM-ing instead of group posting for privacy, syncing calendars, speaking through glasses rather than car media, curating evolving group conversations, and helping his daughter learn while keeping parents informed.

sections.title: Three aspects of group chat agents
sections.summary: He identifies three core challenges: the guard (security), memory, and routing of information to the correct end user.

sections.title: Securing an agentic system: Jetou
sections.summary: He argues agentic systems cannot be secured like LLMs because they interact with tools and external content, vastly expanding the attack surface across web pages, emails, GitHub issues, and group messages. He names this security layer Jetou after a mythological character.

sections.title: When two safe skills collide
sections.summary: He references a paper showing that two individually safe skills—an OCR module and a reporting module—can become malignant when running together, with approximately 90% of attacks exploiting this combination. The OCR extracts information while the reporting agent leaks PII to a third party.

sections.title: Designing a guard at the action boundary
sections.summary: His defense lets the agent read everything but places a deterministic guard at the action boundary—reading secrets, exporting data, executing commands. The guard classifies actions as benign, needs-approval, or blocked using traditional NLP or regex approaches.

sections.title: A small model with per-user LoRA adapters
sections.summary: He fine-tunes an SLM with LoRA adapters to separate the data channel from the instruction channel, releasing only benign information. Benchmarked on inspect agent, the naive approach is at 50% (coin flip) while the learned model improves on that. The learned model catches interspersed-dot prompt injections that regex misses.

sections.title: Designing memory for groups: atomic facts and relevance scoring
sections.summary: He introduces memory as the second core challenge. Rather than naively storing everything and compacting, he advocates extracting atomic information bits relevant to future conversations. Auto-rators evaluate extraction quality, temporal relevance, hierarchical relationships, and retrieval accuracy, potentially using graph-based organization. For what to store and forget, he references the 'learning what not to forget' paper and its continual relevance scorer that adapts as group context evolves, enabling knowledge-based compaction that saves tokens. He notes KV caching challenges when serving stored memories and emphasizes that group memory design differs from personal agent memory.

sections.title: Privacy as a social contract with per-user adapters
sections.summary: He frames a shared assistant as a new social contract: information is public or private depending on context, not content alone—a grocery list is benign for all, but salary or health information becomes private or public depending on the room. His approach uses a shared memory layer with per-user LoRA adapters that bake permissions into the model via machine learning rather than code, referencing the 'user as an engram' paper for scaling. He also notes group agents tend to be over-proactive and proposes training a classifier to determine when an agent should speak.

sections.title: Conclusion: Three pillars for group agent harnesses
sections.summary: He concludes that group agent harnesses must address at least three additional things: the security layer (the gate that filters information based on context), memory design and harness, and routing of information to responsible parties.

technologies.label: Jataayu Action Authorization Architecture
technologies.summary: Jataayu is a deterministic action authorization layer for AI agents developed by Sai Krishna Rallabandi. Rather than gating input, it gates the effect — placing guards at the action boundary where agent actions produce side effects (reading secrets, exporting data, executing commands). Actions are classified as benign, needs-approval, or blocked. The architecture includes InboundGuard with 55+ regex patterns and an LLM slow path, OutboundGuard for PII/privacy and credential detection, surface profiles with trust levels and risk multipliers for different communication surfaces (group chat, DM, glasses), and integration as an MCP gateway proxy. Named after the mythological bird Jatayu from the Hindu epic Ramayana. The transcript consistently mishears it as 'Jetou'; web verification through the speaker's first-party GitHub repository and LinkedIn posts confirms the correct spelling.
technologies.role: Central to the security pillar, occupying approximately 40% of the talk by transcript section count. The speaker describes its action-boundary guard design, three-tier action classification, supplementary SLM layer for prompt injection detection, and the specific skill collision attack vector it defends against.

technologies.label: Per-User LoRA Permission and Injection-Detection Adapters
technologies.primary: Per-user LoRA permission adapters for context-dependent privacy
technologies.summary: Per-user LoRA adapters are trained on top of a shared model so that each user's permissions are baked into their adapter's weights rather than enforced by application code. This encodes context-dependent privacy policy through machine learning: the same information (e.g., salary, health data) is public or private depending on conversational context, not content. The speaker references the 'user as an engram' paper for scaling this approach. A closely related use of LoRA fine-tuning appears in the security pillar, where an SLM with LoRA adapters separates the data channel from the instruction channel to detect prompt injections that regex misses, including interspersed-dot attacks (e.g., 'I.Li.K.E.this'). On the inspect agent benchmark, the naive regex approach performs at 50% (coin flip) while the LoRA-tuned SLM improves on that baseline. The speaker also proposes a trained classifier using a similar approach to determine when group agents should speak versus remain silent, addressing over-proactiveness.
technologies.role: Central to both the security pillar (SLM injection detection surpassing 50% baseline, catching interspersed-dot attacks) and the privacy pillar (per-user LoRA adapters baking permissions into model weights). The speaker frames this as encoding privacy policy through ML rather than code, referencing the 'user as an engram' paper.

technologies.label: Learned Relevance Eviction (LRE) for Agent Memory Compaction
technologies.primary: Learned Relevance Eviction (LRE) / Continual Relevance Scoring
technologies.summary: Learned Relevance Eviction (LRE) is a continual relevance scoring method referenced in the talk for managing group agent memory. The technique learns which units of agent history are load-bearing for future conversations and retains them via verbatim extraction while discarding low-relevance units. In the talk's context, this enables knowledge-based compaction that saves tokens as group context evolves, rather than naively storing everything and compacting uniformly. The verified source paper (arXiv 2606.20954, published June 2026) describes LRE as a CPU-only, language-model-free scorer, making it practical for real-time memory management. The speaker pairs this with atomic fact extraction (extracting discrete, self-contained facts rather than raw transcripts) and auto-rators that evaluate extraction quality, temporal relevance, and hierarchical relationships, potentially using graph-based organization for retrieval. He also notes KV-cache challenges when serving stored memories with unconventional modifications to the serving pipeline.
technologies.role: Central to the memory pillar. The speaker references the 'learning what not to forget' paper as the basis for continual relevance scoring, which together with atomic fact extraction and auto-rators forms his proposed group memory design. He contrasts this approach with naive store-everything-and-compact strategies.

technologies.label: SuchiLM / Judith Agent Platform
technologies.summary: SuchiLM is the LLM underlying the Judith agent, based on a modified Qwen3 model. The Judith agent was deployed for approximately 8 months among the speaker's friends and family across WhatsApp groups, Discord channels, private DMs, and $40 smart glasses, serving as the case study for the talk's three-pillar group agent architecture. The glasses deployment integrates Whisper for ASR, Flite for TTS, Qwen2.5 for image processing, and the modified Qwen3-based SuchiLM as the core LLM — details not enumerated in the talk but verified through the speaker's February 2026 LinkedIn post. The speaker's CMU homepage references Judith as a personal project. The agent's real-world deployment demonstrates group-specific challenges: DM-ing instead of group posting for privacy, calendar syncing across users, glasses-based interaction, conversation curation, and child learning support. The talk uses these deployment experiences to motivate the redesign of security, memory, and information routing around the group rather than bolting multi-user support onto single-user architectures.
technologies.role: The Judith agent is the central case study throughout the entire talk, with deployment examples (DM-ing for privacy, calendar syncing, glasses interaction, conversation curation, child learning support) illustrating each of the three architectural challenges. The agent's 8-month deployment provides empirical evidence for the talk's thesis that single-user agent assumptions break in group settings.
